rc.title: Reading Comprehension
rc.directions: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow. Choose the most appropriate option.
rc.passage: Of all the casualties of the digital age, the most quietly devastating is our capacity for sustained attention. A century ago, an educated reader could lose himself in a dense novel for hours; today, even the committed reader finds his eyes drifting after a few paragraphs, his hand reaching, almost involuntarily, for the glowing rectangle in his pocket. The problem is not that we read less — by some measures we read more than ever — but that we read shallowly, skating across the surface of a thousand fragments rather than diving into the depths of a single idea. Technology companies, it must be said, have engineered this restlessness deliberately; their profits depend on our distraction. Yet to blame the machines entirely would be too convenient. The deeper truth is that sustained attention has always been difficult, always demanded a discipline that most of us would rather avoid. The screen did not create our impatience; it merely gave it a permanent home.

questions.question: Q1. Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The financial success of technology companies in the digital age
The decline of our ability to concentrate deeply on a single idea
The superiority of old novels over modern forms of writing
The harmful physical effects of reading for too many hours
questions.answer: The decline of our ability to concentrate deeply on a single idea
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly returns to the loss of 'sustained attention' and the habit of reading 'shallowly'. The other options are details or distortions, not the main concern.

questions.question: Q2. According to the author, the responsibility for our distraction:
options: lies entirely with individual readers and their laziness
is shared between technology and our own nature
cannot be determined from the available evidence
questions.answer: is shared between technology and our own nature
questions.explanation: The author admits companies 'engineered this restlessness' but adds that 'to blame the machines entirely would be too convenient', since 'sustained attention has always been difficult'. So responsibility is shared.

questions.question: Q3. As used in the first sentence, the word 'casualties' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: A 'casualty' is something destroyed or lost. The trap is confusing it with 'casual' (informal). The context — 'the most quietly devastating' — confirms the sense of loss.

questions.question: Q4. The author states that the real problem with modern reading is that:
options: people read far fewer books than they once did
people read shallowly rather than deeply
modern novels have become far too dense
technology has made reading almost impossible
questions.answer: people read shallowly rather than deeply
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says 'The problem is not that we read less ... but that we read shallowly.' Option (a) is directly contradicted.

questions.question: Q5. The overall tone of the passage can best be described as:
questions.explanation: The author criticises the loss of attention but resists easy blame ('too convenient'), weighing both sides. That balance is reflective and critical, not purely angry or indifferent.

cloze.title: Cloze Test
cloze.directions: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank. (SSC CGL 2024 PYQ)
cloze.passage: The beginning of the story is (1)______ in its presentation but (2)______ the style eases out and becomes haunting in its simplicity. The author brings out the human elements in his story. This common element of sympathy and sacrifice is given a new (3)______ by the old artist who shows by his last desperate act that one can be a hero for one day if only one cares (4)______. O Henry's treatment of his material is balanced and controlled, a fine (5)______ of humour and pathos.

questions.question: Blank (1):
questions.explanation: 'Quaint' means charmingly old-fashioned or unusual, fitting a distinctive presentation. 'Prone/habitual' suggest tendency; 'delectable' means tasty — both off-context.

questions.question: Blank (2):
questions.explanation: The style 'eases out' over time, so 'gradually' (slowly, over time) is correct.

questions.question: Blank (3):
questions.explanation: A 'new dimension' means a new aspect or perspective added to the theme of sympathy and sacrifice.

questions.question: Blank (4):
questions.explanation: 'cares enough' conveys sufficient concern to act heroically. The other words do not fit the idea of sufficiency.

questions.question: Blank (5):
questions.explanation: 'A fine blend of humour and pathos' means a smooth combination of the two — exactly the intended meaning.

parajumble.title: Para Jumbles
parajumble.directions: Each sentence has been split into four parts (P, Q, R, S) given in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges them into a meaningful sentence.

items.explanation: S (subject 'Curiosity,') → Q (the parenthetical 'far from being a distraction,') → P ('is in fact the engine') → R ('that drives every genuine discovery'). Reads: 'Curiosity, far from being a distraction, is in fact the engine that drives every genuine discovery.'

parts.label: Q
parts.text: although he had every reason to despair,

items.explanation: Q (concession clause) → P ('he chose instead') → R ('to confront his misfortune') → S ('with quiet dignity'). The 'although' clause must open the sentence.

parts.label: P
parts.text: which scholars had long believed lost,

items.explanation: R (subject) → P (relative clause describing it) → Q (main verb 'was discovered in the cellar') → S ('of a crumbling monastery').

parts.label: R
parts.text: What begins as a harmless habit

items.explanation: R (subject 'What begins as a harmless habit') → Q ('can, if left unchecked,') → P ('gradually harden into an addiction') → S ('that governs one's life').

parts.label: R
parts.text: has been deceiving him all along

items.explanation: Inverted structure: Q ('Not until the final page') → P ('does the reader realise') → S ('that the unreliable narrator') → R ('has been deceiving him all along').
